newsitem.title: USA: Calif. wage changes to save millions - state.
newsitem.headline: Calif. wage changes to save millions - state.

text.p: Reforms to California's wage regulations, which went into effect on Monday, should save local governments in the state millions of dollars each year, state officials said.

"Local governments, school, fire health and other special districts can now begin to realize cost savings and the ability to provide more and improved services to the taxpayers and consumers of their services," said Lloyd Aubry Jr., director of the California Department of Industrial Relations.
The changes repealed a provision in the rules that had called for payment of higher wages on certain projects. The reforms also changed the way prevailing wages are calculated.
The state's prevailing wage rules now parallel those of the federal government and most other states, Aubry said.
California Gov. Pete Wilson had asked the Department of Industrial Relations to pursue the changes because attempts to reform the rules through the legislature had failed.
After a series of public hearings, the regulations were approved by the Office of Administrative Law, and were filed with the Secretary of State in late December.
The Department of Industrial Relations said the new regulations would result in rates that more accurately reflect prevailing wages.
"The reforms will ultimately offer millions of dollars in taxpayer savings on public works contracts in California, with particular impact in rural areas," Aubry said.
Prevailing wage laws require the payment of minimum wage rates equal to those prevailing in a given community. The rules apply to state and local public works projects.
Local jurisdictions determined prevailing wages until 1976 when the function was centralized under the Department of Industrial Relations.
